stories.title: Your Perception Of Time Is, In Fact, Warped
stories.summary: The post Your Perception Of Time Is, In Fact, Warped appeared first on NOEMA .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
We keep marveling at how fast the years go by. The deeper problem is that we’re forgetting them — and losing the quiet, boring moments where memory forms.

Mike Mariani is a writer and journalist based in the D.C. area, and the author of “What Doesn’t Kill Us Makes Us,” published in August 2022 by Penguin Random House

We’ve long been ensorcelled by the passage of time. Puckered leaves fluttering from the spidery arms of barren trees. Grains of sand tumbling through the delicate neck of an hourglass. A curved cornice perched over a snow-covered mountain, awaiting an avalanche to bring it down. These evocative emblems of seasons, hours, and the vicissitudes they leave in their wake speak to the bittersweet relationship we’ve cultivated with this unit of measurement.

Whether in Proustian reveries, digital photo libraries, or the watchful doppelgänger that gazes out at us each morning, ever-so-slightly altered, we’re inclined to a tender wistfulness toward time — the persistent awareness that, however fast or slow, it’s forever slipping through our fingers.

But lately, our relationship to the months, years and decades that landscape our lives has shifted in some unsettling ways. Instead of regarding the passage of time with introspection or melancholy, many of us now observe it with a mounting sense of alarm.

You don’t have to look very far to find ample evidence that we are experiencing a metaphysical crack-up around time. There’s a growing conviction among people from all walks of life that time is moving faster than it did several decades ago — or even prior to the Covid pandemic. While this belief crept into the zeitgeist like a sly, slinking fog, the refrains are now so pervasive that they’ve started to supplant idle chatter on the weather. Our focus has shifted from rejoicing in cloudless days or grousing over gloomy skies to fixating on the dizzying speed at which our lives are hurtling by.

This is particularly evident on sites like Reddit, where users now regularly commiserate over how rapidly the years are passing. A farmer whose work cycles alongside the seasons “can’t believe how fast this year has gone.” A middle school teacher recounts how she finds herself “having these conversations with students … who are perturbed by the speed of life.” Perhaps most tellingly, for a programmer, the “pandemic years blurred together, and everything after feels compressed, like one long season instead of separate years.” Civilizational events, including not only Covid but also climate change, large-scale armed conflict and the rise of AI “have piled up so quickly that it feels like we’re living through multiple decades at once.”

In recent years, these stray observations have coalesced into a chorus. Everyone from Boomers to Zoomers is mystified at how the passage of time has sped up, and feels disoriented by the strange velocity that’s colored how we’re living through the 2020s. But to hear these stifled laments is also to observe the absurdity of contemporary American life: While so many of us agree that our relationship to time has been warped, our collective response has been to shake it off and move on. It’s as though we all started losing our depth perception at the same time — crashing into road medians, pratfalling down staircases — and instead of resolving to rectify the predicament, we’ve simply resigned ourselves to daily collisions and collapses.

In some ways, the scale of this phenomenon resembles an episode of mass cognitive dissonance, or even a population-level folie à deux. It’s worth asking if something about our internal mechanisms for gauging the passage of time has changed — or been irrevocably thrown out of sync with human timekeeping and the atomic clocks we’ve structured civilization around for nearly a century. Or, alternatively, perhaps the pandemic spoiled our capacity to judge duration, expanding and contracting our sense of time over and over until the fabric grew loose and rippled, an undifferentiated mass of fibers stretched into a form we no longer recognize.

A Theory Of Relativity

Scientists and academics have been grappling with some of these questions since the 19th century. In the 1890s, renowned French philosopher Paul Janet proposed that human beings experience time in proportion to their age. When we’re 10 years old, one year is fully 10% of our entire lifetimes; as a result, we process it with slow, substantive vividness. When we’re 50 years old, on the other hand, that same year represents only 2% of our lives, and we experience it with corresponding ephemerality and diminished gravitas. Janet’s theory would come to be known as “logarithmic time perception,” a reference to the measurement scale that represents mathematical figures proportionately (it’s sometimes referred to as the “time alive” theory).

William James picked up where Janet left off, positing in “Principles of Psychology” that time moves more slowly for young people, who slingshot themselves into fresh experiences every day. “Apprehension is vivid, retentiveness strong, and our recollections of that time, like those of a time spent in rapid and interesting travel, are of something intricate, multitudinous, and long-drawn-out,” he writes.

“You don’t have to look very far to find ample evidence that we are experiencing a metaphysical crack-up around time.”

James argues that the absorbing episodes children and teenagers so often find themselves in give the brain more to chew on — both in the moment and long after the moment’s passed. Because their exploits are consistently novel and stimulating, young people have the retrospective sensation that those specific intervals of time were fuller, deeper, more robust.

As we grow older, however, we become more immersed in patterns and routines, without the same opportunities to process new information, foster fresh skills or feel our way through unfamiliar circumstances that galvanize our intellects. We’re living by rote, so to speak, and our consciousness slides into a more dulled, dampened state. As a result, James notes, “the days and the weeks smooth themselves out in recollection to contentless units, and the years grow hollow and collapse.”

Though James was writing before the fields of neuroscience and psychology were even established — Freud had yet to publish his first book — his insights have been embraced by researchers more than a century later. Many of them now argue that the way we gauge time is inextricably linked to how active and engaged our brains are, and the extent to which we form memories.

When we’re seeing, hearing, touching and tasting exotic sights, sounds, surfaces and foods that arouse our senses, we’re far more likely to lay down new memories. Those recollections inform how we retrospectively evaluate the passage of time, giving it that languorous, “long-drawn-out” quality James described. “We only remember things which are novel or exciting or scary or have some visceral meaning to them,” Luke Jones, a psychologist at the University of Manchester, explained to me. “And your retrospective perception of duration is based on memory.”

But while we’ve long established that humans perceive time in an elastic, subjective way, that knowledge could not have prepared us for the Covid pandemic. That generational event bowed and buckled the way so many of us experience those hourglasses and cornices, swapping out placid reflection for consternation and dread. Over three years of lockdowns, quarantines and the claustrophobic monotony they inspired, countless Americans told anyone who would listen how different time felt to them. The weeks and months, we stammered, felt “stretched,” “warped,” “blurred.”

In 2023, researchers at Baylor University set out to legitimize these anecdotes. A team of sociologists published a study using Gallup data collected at the height of the pandemic to analyze how people perceived time during the period. The authors found that Americans experienced “time disorientation” in multiple directions, with time speeding up, slowing down and days blending together to the point of indistinguishability.

Another study of Uruguayan university students, published in “Time & Society” in 2022, found that 80% of students surveyed felt time had either sped up or slowed down during the pandemic. These findings were replicated in other parts of the world, including Argentina and Iraq . The co-authors of the “Time & Society” paper also noted an intriguing irony: In instances where excessive free time caused by lockdowns or other public health measures led to boredom, “time would be slow in the moment, but looking back on the experience retrospectively, people would feel that time flew.”

This points to a crucial aspect of time perception, one that continues to captivate me: We gauge the speed of time based on one set of factors in the moment — how engaged or stimulated we are — while using a distinct set of criteria to evaluate it retrospectively (the degree to which we formed memories). People trapped in their homes during the pandemic with little to do suffered a worst-case scenario, temporally speaking: the emptiness of their days slowed them to a crawl, while the insipid repetition of their experiences yielded few memories, causing wide swaths of time to, as James puts it, “grow hollow and collapse.”

When I spoke to Marc Wittmann, one of the 2022 study’s co-authors and a time perception researcher at the Institute for Frontier Areas in Psychology and Mental Health in Germany, he explained that the lack of distinct markers during the pandemic made each day look exactly alike, contributing to time disorientation. “Every day was the same,” he said. “Monday used to be the day you went skating, Tuesday was the day you spent with your friends. We used to have something associated with each day.” But all of this disappeared during global lockdowns, he said. Wittmann calls this “Blursday.”

“We’re living by rote, so to speak, and our consciousness slides into a more dulled, dampened state.”

The surge in time disorientation so many of us experienced during the pandemic came to be known as the “2020 effect.” The abrupt upheaval and subsequent tedium of restrictive, repetitive routines in those years led to the sensation of days bleeding into each other, time “stretching” and people losing the ability to recall events sequentially — as though our memories were shuffled and rearranged during a game of three-card monte.

But the most relevant question in 2026 isn’t whether the pandemic influenced how we experience time. A raft of academic papers demonstrate that it clearly did. The question now is whether our perception of time ever snapped back to the way it was before that generational event.

The Internal Clock Fallacy

To determine why our internal clocks sped up over the past few years, it helps to understand exactly what we mean by “internal clocks.” For years, time perception researchers have been trying to explain how human beings subjectively gauge duration. But it’s proven to be a stubborn riddle. One reason for this is that we have no organ or system dedicated to sensing time. Instead, as one 2016 paper puts it , “Psychological time is an abstraction, a construct or epiphenomenon of our mind’s functioning that we create in order to explain the coherence of events.”

Nevertheless, researchers were convinced for years that humans possessed a specific mechanism for measuring time — a theory referred to as the “internal clock model.” Though the model served as a convenient explanation for how humans tell time, scientists eventually grew skeptical of it. “Back then, there was a very anthropocentric model that was suspiciously similar to actual man-made clocks,” said Dean Buonomano, a neuroscientist at the University of California, Los Angeles. “You have some oscillator ticking away at some frequency, and then counting the time units, much like clocks work.” Another problem with the internal clock model was that scientists struggled to find hard evidence for its existence. As Warrick Roseboom, a psychologist at the University of Sussex, told me, “Researchers were just like, ‘Oh, you have a clock in your brain. We just need to find where the clock in your brain is.’”

But scientists never found the clock, and for some the model lost its credibility. Meanwhile, Roseboom and other academics began exploring alternative theories. In 2022, he and several colleagues at the University of Sussex published the results of a study that showed participants short videos to determine whether there was a relationship between the way we process the world around us and how we gauge the passage of time.

In the experiment, the amount of activity the videos elicited in participants’ brains was strongly correlated with their subjective sense of how much time passed. When the participants detected more happening in the videos, it triggered large changes in brain activity associated with visual processing, creating the sensation that more time had gone by. Roseboom and his co-authors concluded that we tell time based on “the accumulation of salient changes in the perceptual processing hierarchy” — or, as co-author Maxine Sherman said when the paper was published, “the brain just ‘counts’ how much ‘stuff’ has happened, which is very intuitive.”

One of the paper’s key takeaways is that our perception of time isn’t based on any fixed sense of duration. We do not, in fact, have an internal clock measuring minutes, hours and days. Instead, we use our external environment as a proxy for the passage of time. The more “stuff” our sensory cortex is picking up on, the more time we register as passing.

This new way of looking at time perception could shed light on why so many people feel like time is speeding up today. We’re inundated with videos, images, notifications and a cavalcade of content 24 hours a day, forcing our brains to contend with far more information than they needed to 10 or 20 years ago. Read Noema in print.

When I reached out to James Hyman, a neuroscientist at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, he felt that applying Roseboom and his co-authors’ new theory of time perception to our current media ecosystem explained why so many people now feel flummoxed by the speed of their lives. “We’re constantly moving onto the next thing,” he said. “And the more things that we experience that cause us to move forward, well, if our brains are only able to tell time by counting things, then we’re jamming lots more things in there.” When we’re flooded with text, images and glowing blue light, our brains are tricked into speeding up the internal proxy mechanisms they use for measuring time. As a result, time feels like it’s moving faster and faster.

“We have no organ or system dedicated to sensing time.”

But the casino-like frenzy of our digital environments is only part of the reason our perception of time is changing. Remember that we assess duration from multiple vantage points, including retrospectively, when we gauge how much time we feel passed during a specific period. When we tell our spouse that “this week flew by,” we’re engaging in retrospective time perception. Arguably the most important variable in those judgments is memory — whether we formed them, how many we formed, how vivid they are.

Memories are the trees, shrubs and undulating peaks that landscape our past, preventing it from hollowing out and collapsing in on itself. (Smooth and featureless as the interior of a spaceship, the pandemic had no landscape, and our memory of it collapsed accordingly.) Because of this variability, retrospective time perception is even more subjective than other forms of time judgment, given its outsized dependence on “things which are novel or exciting or scary or have some visceral meaning to them.” The memories that stem from those stimuli are our footprints in the snow, giving our past the solidity and verisimilitude that would otherwise blow away in the past’s enveloping whiteout.

Our memories are the key to the central irony of our supersaturated world. Roseboom’s theory posits that time spent in an environment overflowing with visual information should feel long and robust. “You would think that because we’re paying more attention to more things, that retrospectively time should feel longer,” Jones noted. “But I think we’ve got the worst of all worlds.” Because while we encounter a glittering constellation of apps, games and videos beckoning us at every turn, eager to light up our sensory cortex, they’re not generating the indelible experiences crucial to forming memories. “When you get to the end of the day, you look back and there’s no meaningful content there. It’s just the same blur, the same stuff, and there’s nothing distinctive about it.”

Wittmann agrees that toggling between apps on our phone and numbing ourselves with Instagram reels can impoverish our retrospective perception of time. “When we’re on digital media, time passes very quickly,” he explained. “You lose yourself. You’re jumping around like mad in these apps, and you can’t put them into memory and later recall them, because the experiences just vanish.”

Browsing, scrolling and swiping are more likely to quiet or even anesthetize our brains than activate them in the ways required to form memories. As a result, spending an hour on TikTok might feel like 10 or 15 minutes, because we don’t have any of the “intricate, multitudinous, and long-drawn-out” sensations that give time depth and fullness. Instead, it all blends together in a turbulent vortex, overwhelming the senses rather than engaging them on the level necessary to endure over time. It’s easy to extrapolate this further and speculate how spending several hours a day on social media distorts our sense of time, giving us the impression that we were awake for just 12 or 13 hours of the day. Over months and years, surrendering this much time to our ersatz digital warrens can lead to a sense of deprivation — a feeling that years have been carved out of our lives.

According to Wittmann and other researchers, social media platforms are uniquely effective at short-circuiting our retrospective time perception. After spending time on these apps, the abstract field our mind’s eye draws from to make sense of recent experiences is left barren, devoid of the evocative wisps we integrate into the hazy memory palace that ultimately serves as our past. Instead, many of us are now confined to a permanent amnesiac present, one throbbing with artificial life but unable to fathom where it came from or where it’s going.

Investigating The Time Warp

The collective sense that time is moving faster today than it has in the past has gained enough traction for scientists to start taking notice. A group of European psychologists has teamed up to form Time Experience in Europe’s Digital Age, abbreviated as TIMED. This research consortium, which includes some of the top time-perception researchers in Germany, Spain, Switzerland and the U.K., is using interviews, questionnaires and experiments to explore how our perception of time is influenced by how we use technology.

TIMED has spent the last three years collecting data from tens of thousands of study participants all over the world, and they’re now sharing the results of that project. In papers published so far, researchers have arrived at a number of important takeaways. First, people who spend more time on devices and social media platforms experience time passing more quickly. In one of their papers, Wittmann and his co-authors cited memory as a key factor in this correlation, with the use of digital technology limiting the breadth of people’s experiences and foreclosing on the events we most often remember.

“The collective sense that time is moving faster today than it has in the past has gained enough traction for scientists to start taking notice.”

“Routine activities such as repeatedly checking apps or prolonged online engagement for professional purposes could reduce the frequency of novel, embodied, and enactive experiences,” they wrote. “This, in turn, results in fewer rich or meaningful events being encoded in autobiographical memory. Consequently, such periods may retrospectively appear less eventful and more compressed, contributing to the feeling that time has passed quickly.”

Unsurprisingly, perhaps, researchers also found that excessive use of technological devices promoted a negative relationship with time. “Participants associated digital technology use with a loss of time, a desire to fill all time, a propensity to forget time and, as a result, a desire to gain greater control of time,” they wrote. Feeling that one’s relationship with time had spun out of control in turn spawned “feelings of guilt, shame, and a lack of self-control.”

Wittmann and his colleagues conducted qualitative interviews for TIMED, and some participants expressed frustration and even helplessness at how devices were transforming their sense of time. “What was really interesting to me was how people constantly talked about digital technology stealing their time,” Ruth Ogden, TIMED’s lead investigator, said. “One of the things that happens when you engage in doom scrolling and other forms of social media is you completely forget about time — time doesn’t exist anymore. So then you massively overextend how long you engage in these activities for.”

But Ogden doesn’t think that technology should be seen as the sole culprit for our warped perceptions of time. The strains in that relationship go deeper than memes, AI slop and infinite scroll, stemming from how modern society frames inert, unproductive states like boredom and “doing nothing.” In TIMED’s interviews, respondents also told Ogden and her colleagues they were uncomfortable with periods of inactivity and felt compelled to use their devices to fill every available gap in their schedule. “What we found through TIMED is that even when people have time, they don’t use it to do nothing,” she told me. “We live in a society that really values constantly being busy and constantly having something to do. We saw this in TIMED through people’s use of digital technology, where every bit of free time was spent on screens.”

If people were more comfortable with intervals that lacked so-called productivity — quiet longueurs, spells of boredom or periods of aimless reflection — they might stand a better chance of expanding and enriching the way they experience time. “It’s in those calm moments where we see a unique pattern of activity in the part of our brain responsible for helping to make our memories,” Hyman said. Those still, empty stretches are when we contemplate our immediate pasts, integrating them into the larger arc of our lives.

We know, however, that these states have been largely vaporized this decade — and only a seismic shift in our values and ideals stands a chance of reclaiming them. In Ogden’s eyes, the dilemma hinges on a simple question: “How do we get people back to being comfortable with doing very little and believing that doing little is not an indication of laziness?”

The Beauty Of Boredom

The stakes of this phenomenon can sometimes seem low. Feeling like time is speeding up is not a “kitchen table issue”; it won’t raise your taxes or make you go hungry. But the TIMED project has demonstrated that people who feel like they’re losing time are genuinely unhappy and even distressed about it. Members of Gen Z, in particular, don’t talk about the quickening pace of their lives with disinterested curiosity or frivolous bemusement — they lament it. When we lose our grip on the passage of time, it can feel like we’re also losing grip on our own lives.

Western culture views time as a currency to be leveraged, channeled and optimized. The societal pressure to perform productivity at all times is so insistent and thrumming that many of us — myself included — have lost the ability to slow down and luxuriate in the inherent slowness of time, the way it oozes forward like honey slithering across a glass jar. When Aldous Huxley was asked about time by an interlocutor in “The Doors of Perception,” his reply was both simple and profound. “There seems to be plenty of it,” he said. Untethered from his ego and all the worldly attachments it clung to, Huxley was able to tap into the spaciousness of existence — an amplitude and abundance that’s permanent and inviolable, if only we still had the freedom to see it.

“When we lose our grip on the passage of time, it can feel like we’re also losing grip on our own lives.”

It’s true that technology has capitalized on this culture of synchronized compliance. The companies that manufacture our devices and make the programs that run on them have wedged themselves into this perverse relationship to productivity, offering the badges and motifs that signify a certain enterprising competence. As Jenny Odell points out in her book, “How to Do Nothing,” there’s a battle playing out “for our time, a colonization of the self by capitalist ideas of productivity and efficiency.” Through these products, we personify the ideals of practicality and industriousness.

The pandemic, too, eventually fed into the hungry zeitgeist of maximizing our output and sacrificing ourselves on the altar of “getting ahead.” The increased use of communications platforms like Slack, Teams and Zoom promoted a porousness between our work and home lives, allowing what Odell calls a “certain nervous feeling, of being overstimulated and unable to sustain a train of thought” to infiltrate spaces long insulated from them.

This explains why many people feel that the way they experienced time during the pandemic never snapped back to how they processed it before Covid. In the aftermath, we became even more tethered to these platforms and other virtual spaces where productivity lingers at a low, insistent hum 24 hours a day. With our minds more anxious and overstimulated, our perception of time never had the chance to return to an earlier, more composed pace.

Further, trends that predated Covid resurfaced as though shot out of a cannon, and the ambient pressure to advance our lots at all costs imbued our culture with a mercenary quality. We were all racing to make more money, afford a home, secure a job, #YOLO at the live events we were unceremoniously robbed of. Amid this competitive turbulence — and the technologies that capitalized on our unease about it — everything started to move faster.

If we accept this premise, then maybe the crisis of time speeding up is not as hopelessly irreversible as it often seems. According to the latest time perception research, the amount of information our brains engage with shapes our subjective sense of how fast time is moving. If we intentionally reduce the stimuli we’re exposing ourselves to in a given day or week, then our brains will gradually slow down. And if our brains slow down, then our perception of time will taper off, too.

For their part, Ogden and other TIMED researchers feel that society has imposed too much responsibility on the individual to limit their use of technology. “Maybe it’s time that we shifted some of that onto the creators,” Ogden said. “The key metric for the success of digital technology is how long users are on it for, and how many people they can get on it for as long as possible. How do we flip that?” While we wait for those larger systemic changes, though, Ogden emphasized the importance of using our devices in a more intentional fashion. “What are you trying to get out of this digital technology use?” she asked. “You need to have an awareness of your own goals.”

In addition to modifying our own individual behavior, however, we also need to change the culture surrounding how we spend our time. That means coming to terms with the reality that boredom and “doing nothing” are neither shameful nor necessary evils. “There is huge value in doing nothing,” Ogden said. “We need to move away from thinking that it’s weird, lazy or slovenly.” Asked how she would spend a perfect holiday, Ogden described something very close to what people now labor so strenuously to avoid. “It would be to go and sit in a square in Italy with a nice glass of wine and watch the world go by.”

In his “Principles of Psychology,” William James invites us to participate in an experiment. “Close your eyes and simply wait to hear somebody tell you that a minute has elapsed,” he writes. The length of that single minute, he explains, will feel overwhelming. “You engulf yourself into its bowels as into those of that interminable first week of an ocean voyage, and find yourself wondering that history can have overcome many such periods in its course.” Those 60 seconds feel so full, James goes on, because “you attend so closely to the mere feeling of the time per se. ” When our senses are engaged and stimulated, time is compressed, disguised, eclipsed. “The feeling of bare time,” however, “is the least stimulating experience we can have.”

We used to tolerate those interminable minutes standing in a crowded grocery line, gazing out the convex glass window of an airplane, waiting for the dull red digits on an oven timer to run down to zero. These are now the endangered species of our day-to-day lives. And they are far more valuable than we ever could have known.

stories.title: A Surge of Marine Heat Waves Threatens to Scramble Ocean Life
stories.summary: Fueled by climate change and a strengthening El Niño, record-setting marine heat waves are gripping oceans worldwide and playing havoc with sea life. Mounting evidence from recent events suggests the damage could be severe and long-lasting, both onshore and off. Read more on E360 →

stories.body:
Waters off the coast of Southern California, where a prolonged marine heat wave is disrupting sea life. Kevin Carter / Getty Images

Fueled by climate change and a strengthening El Niño, record-setting marine heat waves are gripping oceans worldwide and playing havoc with sea life. Mounting evidence from recent events suggests the damage could be severe and long-lasting, both onshore and off.

By Jim Robbins • September 3, 2026

Facebook

Twitter

LinkedIn

Email

The common octopus is a warm water species that usually lives in the temperate waters of the Mediterranean. But last year, octopus larvae hitchhiked across the English Channel attached to plankton, resulting in an octopus bloom off England’s coast. This year, the bloom is the largest it’s been in 75 years.

Normally, octopus larvae that drift into cold waters die. But this year’s bloom, experts say, is the result of an unusually intense marine heat wave off of Devon and Cornwall, which raised water temperatures up to 9 degrees F above normal.

The change in species has been a boon for local fishers selling octopus into the lucrative European export market. (Octopus landings along the U.K.’s southwest coast were roughly 7,700 percent higher than usual in 2025.) And while the invasion has slashed the catch of scallops, lobster, and crab, it has boosted numbers of seals, conger eels, and dolphins, which eat octopus. The warming, in combination with abundant prey, has also drawn bluefin tuna and sharks to British waters for the first time in decades.

“It has completely shaken up the food chain,” said Bryce Stewart, a senior research fellow at the UK’s Marine Biological Association, which has been studying the phenomenon. While this kind of bloom has happened here before, he said, this one is different. During past surges, the return of cold water killed off the octopuses. This time, the octopuses aren’t dying. They’re reproducing.

And the heat wave continues.

An estimated 82 percent of the world’s oceans are currently experiencing marine heat waves.

Globally, marine heat waves — prolonged periods of unusually warm water — are becoming more common, more intense, longer lasting, and more widespread, experts say . This year, ocean heat is unusually severe, setting new temperature records . According to Global Climate Risks, a nonprofit created by scientists to publicize the effects of climate change, an estimated 82 percent of the world’s oceans are currently experiencing marine heat waves. Evidence from recent hot spells suggests the impacts on sea life could be profound and long-lasting.

Ocean fevers can rearrange marine ecosystems, drive fish to move into deeper, colder layers of the sea, trigger coral bleaching, and cause widespread marine die-offs. They can increase the severity and number of algal blooms, which harm fish, shellfish, marine mammals, and birds. And they can cause extreme weather events, like tropical storms and hurricanes, and upend fishing and tourism.

To officially be called a heat wave, temperatures must rise above the 90th percentile of normal seasonal variation for five consecutive days. While marine heat waves do occur naturally, climate scientists say anthropogenic warming has exacerbated them. According to NOAA scientists, oceans have absorbed more than 90 percent of the excess heat produced by human-caused global warming. One recent study found that, since 1940, warming has led to a threefold increase in the number of days per year with extreme heat at the ocean surface.

Marine heat waves in August. Warmer colors indicate greater severity. NOAA

Climate warming and marine heat waves are separate phenomena with different effects. Ocean warming is gradual and allows more time for species to adapt and evolve. Marine heat waves are acute and produce rapid and extreme changes that give organisms little time to adapt. But the long-term warming trend is making ocean heat more severe.

Climate change has raised the temperature of the waters off the U.K. by around 2 degrees F above average in the last six decades, worsening this year’s record heat. Records have fallen elsewhere in Europe as well. “We find it’s the most extreme July marine heat wave conditions for the Western Mediterranean, the Celtic Region, and for the Bay of Biscay and Iberian Peninsula,” said Catherine Gregory, a climate scientist at the University of Bern.

The Pacific has warmed in northern regions by almost 2 degrees F and is currently experiencing the world’s largest marine heat wave, which sprawls over more than 24 million square miles. And in the central and eastern Pacific, things are bound to get worse. This year’s El Niño is expected to be the strongest in living memory — it has already spiked sea temperatures far earlier in the year than expected — and scientists fear it will expand the size and intensity of the two existing marine heat waves off the California coast. Based on studies of past heat waves — in particular, an event known as the Blob, the largest marine heat wave on global record, which dramatically raised temperatures in the eastern Pacific between 2014 and 2016 — scientists are warily watching the warming ocean, anticipating a cascade of severe impacts both onshore and off.

Seabirds in South America have been dying in large numbers, a trend experts say is linked to higher ocean temperatures.

The Blob began to form in the fall of 2013, when a persistent high-pressure ridge greatly reduced the cool winter winds that normally blow over the eastern Pacific. Without that cooling, the sun created a very large body of very warm water. In 2014, ocean temperatures were 7 degrees F above average, and the cold nutrient-rich water that normally coursed along the West Coast disappeared.

The ecological changes were legion. In 2015, researcher Ric Brodeur was monitoring populations of shrimp-like krill, which form the base of the marine food chain, expecting his sampling nets to be full. Instead, they were almost empty. “You could fit all the krill from the trip into a little plastic bag,” he said.

The lack of food caused humpback whale numbers in the North Pacific to drop by an estimated 7,000 — or 20 percent of the population. Many females became emaciated, which reduced calf survival and caused a reproductive decline that didn’t begin to reverse until 2021, five years after the Blob had officially ended.

While many anomalies caused by the unusually warm water were temporary, some were not. The Blob — which at times approached 10 degrees F higher than average — caused large-scale and long-term ecosystem changes, some of which persist to this day. Researchers are concerned that today’s warming waters will compound the damage caused by previous marine heat waves.

A diver surveys bleached corals off the coast of Koh Tao in Thailand, which was hit by a marine heat wave in 2024. Scientists are worried that record ocean heat this year will further harm corals. Lillian Suwanrumpha / AFP via Getty Images

One of the most egregious of those earlier changes was the die-off of kelp forests along thousands of miles of coast, from Baja California to as far north as British Columbia. Kelp complexes are some of the most dynamic and biologically productive ecosystems on Earth, the “underwater rainforests” of temperate and Arctic coastal oceans. They offer food, nursery grounds, and shelter from predators and rough currents to hundreds of marine species. Kelp canopies, which consist of rubbery floating fronds, are home to sea otters, seabirds, and juvenile fish, while abalone, sea urchins, lobsters, and octopus live on or near the seafloor.

“The Pacific kelp forest has lasted for millions of years,” said Melissa Carter, a biological oceanographer with UC San Diego’s Scripps Institution of Oceanography, thanks to upwellings of cold water along the coast. “But it has a specific temperature threshold where it falls apart and it can’t survive. And everything that lives on the coast depends on that ecosystem.”

One study found that during the Blob, overall kelp cover dropped considerably: Northern California was hardest hit, with 95 percent of its kelp wiped out. The loss of kelp reshaped the entire food web, decimating red abalone populations, which were already in trouble, and prompting the state of California to extend its ban on recreational fishing of the species at least until April 2036.

One of the largest algal blooms in history now stretches from Southern California to the coast of British Columbia.

The Blob also severely impacted seabirds. Half of Alaska’s common murres — some 4 million birds — starved to death as warmer currents disrupted migrations of anchovies, sardines, and other forage fish. “Recent population abundance estimates since then have found no evidence of recovery,” the authors of a 2024 study of the murres concluded, “suggesting that the heatwave may have led to an ecosystem shift.”

Current marine heat waves are already taking a toll. Dead and dying birds, including California brown pelicans, loons, and grebes, are turning up again on Southern California beaches. “We’re seeing cormorants walk to shore and then just die within the hour,” Tammy Russell, a researcher at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, told the Associated Press, “and we’re seeing it happening across the whole coast.” Seabirds along South America’s Pacific coast have been dying in large numbers in recent months, and experts have linked the fatalities to higher ocean temperatures.

Researchers are concerned that current record-setting ocean temperatures, intensified by the strengthening El Niño, will further harm corals. Bleaching occurs when rising water temperatures, in addition to other stressors like pollution and overexposure to sunlight, spur corals to release their symbiotic algae, which harvest energy for them. A bleaching event that lasted from early 2023 until mid-2025 affected more than 84 percent of the world’s coral reef areas. In a major report that was just released, Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network researchers warn that coral reefs around the world are seeing a rapid increase in bleaching and that recovery windows between disturbance events are narrowing.

Veterinarian Jennifer Russell treats an ailing pelican at SeaWorld in San Diego. Rehabilitation centers have cared for hundreds of emaciated seabirds amid a marine heat wave in Southern California. Gregory Bull / AP Photo

Marine heat waves can affect conditions throughout the water column. When a cap of warm water forms at the ocean’s surface, it prevents vertical mixing and can promote the growth of harmful algal species. The explosion of aquatic organisms depletes oxygen in the water, blocks sunlight, and can release harmful toxins into the air and water.

One of the largest algal blooms in history now stretches from Southern California to the coast of British Columbia. The bloom is dominated by an alga called Pseudo-nitzschia , which multiplies faster and becomes more toxic in warmer water. The alga produces a neurotoxin called domoic acid that is responsible for killing hundreds of California’s sea lions, whales, and porpoises.

It is a perilous moment for the world’s oceans as temperatures hit levels never seen in modern times. And scientists fear the impacts of earlier warming events are only a prologue for what lies ahead.

“The Blob was extreme, the warmest we’ve ever seen anything in 110 years,” said Carter, of Scripps. “We are definitely along the same trend now, and the number of marine heat wave days we’ve [already] seen are exactly on par with 2015. This is a new Blob.”

stories.body:
Embryonic gene editing tightens the feedback loop between cultural and biological evolution. The species-level effects remain unclear, but some families are already buying a potential genetic advantage that others can’t.

Brigida D’Agostino is a Los Angeles-based news anchor and journalist covering what happens when technology changes the arrangements that shape everyday life, from reproduction and work to family and government.

Five years ago, I sat in my OB-GYN’s office, three months pregnant, reading a stack of consent forms for noninvasive prenatal testing (NIPT) to find out whether my unborn daughter might have chromosomal abnormalities that would come with lifelong health problems. I wanted the test because I was 36 and my pregnancy was considered “geriatric” — the health system trying to convince me that something was wrong. I wiped the ultrasound goo off my still-flat belly and scribbled my signature on the forms.

By the time my daughter was born, a newer kind of genetic screening service had reached the market: polygenic embryo screening, which ranks embryos developed using in vitro fertilization (IVF) by adding up thousands of tiny genetic variants to estimate the risk of disease or the likelihood of traits in ways that were not available before. The first company to commercialize the service was Genomic Prediction through its LifeView test in 2019. Sam Altman was an early investor. Nucleus Genomics is another company doing similar work.

These companies’ marketing suggests that, for a price, you can design and optimize your child before embryonic implantation. The company Orchid Health charges $2,500 to screen each embryo. That’s on top of one IVF cycle, which starts at around $15,000 . Nucleus bundles embryo screening and IVF into a plan with a four-month minimum, costing about $40,000. The Nucleus website advertises its services as “Modern IVF to give your baby the best start.” The company’s tests screen parents for thousands of genetic disorders and traits they could pass to their children, and scan embryos for diseases and other characteristics. An image of its web app shows a report card on a mobile phone titled “Kids’ most likely traits.” The traits are listed like settings. Height: 5 feet 8 inches. Eye color: hazel. IQ: +2 points. BMI: below average. Muscle strength: average. The American Society for Reproductive Medicine’s ethics and practice committees concluded in December 2025 that polygenic embryo screening is unproven and should not be used clinically at this time. Nucleus’s FAQ says it is “built on validated, peer-reviewed research” and already used in IVF clinics across the U.S. and globally.

Today, doctors and scientists can screen embryos for more traits than ever before. Researchers are also getting better at editing their genes. In June, Columbia University researchers reported in a preprint (not yet peer-reviewed) that they had edited early human embryos with what The New York Times called “unprecedented accuracy” and far less chromosome damage than earlier CRISPR-Cas9 experiments. The technique, called base editing, isn’t ready for reproductive use yet, according to Dieter Egli, the Columbia geneticist who led the research. Nucleus’s chief clinical officer co-authored the study.

Silicon Valley’s interest in reproductive technology is only growing. Altman has backed Preventive, a startup researching embryo editing. Peter Thiel’s Founders Fund and Anne Wojcicki, a co-founder of 23andMe, have also invested in embryo screening firms .

Imagine: report cards for two embryos, each hinting at the person they might become. One apparently has an elevated risk of the melanoma that runs in your family. The other is more likely to share your green eyes. A mini you. Which do you choose? I asked myself this question and made my choice in seconds, but later it started to bother me, even though it was a hypothetical.

What Culture Does For Evolution

Humans adapt through two systems. We adapt through biological evolution, which allows us to inherit genes slowly over generations. And we adapt through cultural evolution, which lets us inherit information quickly so we can feed ourselves, build houses and learn language without waiting for new genes to arrive.

Arizona State University anthropologist Charles Perreault’s 2026 study found that cultural evolution allowed humans to colonize the globe in less than 1% of the time it would have taken through biological evolution alone. Culture, he argued, “enabled the rapid and cumulative acquisition of adaptive behaviors and technologies” that allowed humans to thrive “while remaining a single species with low genetic diversity.” I wondered whether these newer reproductive technologies might let cultural preferences change human evolution on a species-wide scale. I also wondered whether they might create a new genetic class, where some families can buy reproductive advantages that other families can’t.

Joseph Henrich, a prominent theorist of gene-culture coevolution, wasn’t convinced. He told me humans have always used cultural preferences to shape the gene pool, just slowly and indirectly over generations. “When we pick a mate, we pick the genes we like,” he said. Humans are incredibly good at reading traits through observation. We watch how a person we’re romantically interested in behaves, how they look. “We are much better than a polygenic score at predicting what parents care about.”

But the market is built to speed up that dynamic and hand it off first to the people who can pay. IVF has already added another point of selection by allowing parents to choose among embryos, but for years there was little to choose because the data was limited. Polygenic screening gives parents much more information than was previously available, including predictions related to appearance, intelligence and health — which are increasingly being framed around optimization rather than treatment.

“What I found was a tighter feedback loop than existed before, and a market sorting who can buy a potential genetic advantage.”

“Embryo selection is super crude because the genes in any polygenic scores are also in scores for known traits and tons of other unknown traits,” Henrich said. Data for these predictions is also drawn largely from people of European ancestry. Guidance published in The American Journal of Human Genetics in 2022 says a score’s accuracy drops when applied to people outside the dataset it was built on. Henrich also said selection won’t have lasting genetic consequences unless the wealthy somehow sealed off their mating pool and married only within it. But the market doesn’t require endogamy to create a genetic class. It only needs enough people who can pay for choices that others leave to chance. Some investors and industry figures are already describing embryo selection in class terms. A partner at Peter Thiel’s Founders Fund who invested in Nucleus told The Washington Post that embryo selection is a “false choice” today but “in the future, it’s the trust fund.” The Wall Street Journal reported that embryo screening company Herasight ’s in-house philosopher said repeated selection over generations could produce an intelligence gap between the “genetically enhanced” and “genetically unenhanced.” “There’s going to be inequality,” he said.

Perreault told me embryo selection is still gene-culture coevolution, but it creates “an unusually tight feedback loop between cultural preferences, reproductive decisions and genetic transmission.” “Life needed 4.54 billion years to find a way to edit itself,” he continued. Once reproductive technologies begin influencing which embryos are implanted, he added, “some cultural choices become biologically ratcheted into future generations.” He compared it to fertility decline and the spread of contraception, neither of which was designed as a population-level evolutionary intervention. But both changed reproductive patterns over generations. Embryo selection, he said, would be “many individually rational decisions that, in aggregate, could reshape the evolutionary composition of a population in ways that no single actor intends or controls.” He said the magnitude of this effect would depend on how widely embryo selection is adopted and which traits parents select for.

Screening lets parents select among embryos without altering them, picking the best of what chance produced. But editing would let parents modify an embryo’s DNA and introduce sequences neither parent carried.

What Else Are We Choosing?

The problem is that we don’t really know what we’re choosing. Genes are more complex than a report card suggests. A single gene or genetic variant can shape several unrelated traits at the same time. Geneticists call it pleiotropy. A trait that looks like a benefit in one place can carry a liability somewhere else.

A 2018 study of more than 3,700 Mensa members found higher self-reported rates of anxiety, autism, ADHD, allergies, asthma and autoimmune conditions than in the general population. The researchers called it the hyper-brain, hyper-body theory. It doesn’t prove high IQ causes those conditions, but it shows how they may be linked.

I’m a good example of why pleiotropy matters. I’m “twice-exceptional,” which means I’m both autistic and intellectually gifted. My life is harder because of this. I get hives, I’ve fainted from anxiety and I have the gift and curse of monotropism, an extreme form of focus on one interest at the expense of everything else. I’ll ignore my needs for food, water, sleep and the bathroom until my body gives out: my stomach growling, hands shaking and eyes burning. I’ll finish a month’s worth of work in two weeks, but my husband and daughter won’t be happy about it. These traits may be linked in ways scientists don’t fully understand. What would my genetic report card have told my parents about me? What traits would have been detected and how would they have been ranked? Would they have seen a mind of high potential ability or someone at risk of anxiety? Given a choice, would they even pick me?

Even if they did, they might not have gotten what they paid for. We may think we’re in control, but, Henrich told me, “It’s far from clear that all that ‘rational’ selection will do anything other than add more randomness.” Read Noema in print.

Editing genes we don’t fully understand also carries a risk. In 2018, news broke that a Chinese scientist named He Jiankui created the first gene-edited babies. He used CRISPR to modify a gene called CCR5 in twin embryos, hoping to make the girls resistant to HIV, since their father was HIV-positive. But the gene may help fight other infections, including severe West Nile virus . The embryos didn’t have the HIV-resistant mutation that He Jiankui intended to introduce. But the changes he made can be passed on to any children the twins have. He Jiankui went to prison. What he did to those girls can’t be undone.

Gene editing suggests that people can optimize their offspring, but we don’t know whether the editing will result in a trait or characteristic the parents or the person or society at large will value. There is no consensus on the optimal body and mind. The traits on Nucleus’s report card reflect the preferences of this moment. “The desirable traits of the 20th century, like IQ, will unlikely be those of most interest in the 21st century,” Henrich told me.

The Moral Choice?

A parent selecting an embryo in 2026 is making a choice for someone who may still be alive in 2086. Cultural preferences can change quickly, but reproductive decisions can have consequences that last generations.

In 1980, the Chinese government implemented a policy limiting most families to one child. The government never told families whether to choose a boy or girl, but Chinese parents consistently selected for sons. One household at a time, it snowballed into a massive gender imbalance. Today, there are over 30 million more men than women. A large portion of surplus men might never have children because of the imbalance.

In Denmark, prenatal screening resulted in a similar population change. In 2004, the Danish government became the first to offer free Down syndrome screening to all pregnant women. The government didn’t tell parents to end their pregnancies. But after screening showed a higher risk and follow-up testing confirmed the condition, most parents did. The number of children born with Down syndrome halved and has held steady ever since.

“Most cultural preferences came and went faster than they could be written into DNA. Reproductive technologies narrow that gap.”

Parents in both countries used prenatal tools that accurately showed them what they were looking for: a pregnancy with a boy or a girl, or a child likely to be born with Down syndrome. Embryo screening doesn’t offer that same certainty. Results are based on probabilities for traits that no one can guarantee, like a lower risk of depression. The other difference is price. Denmark’s screening was free, and China’s policy was a national directive. Embryo screening with IVF is expensive.

We tend to draw moral lines around these choices as if our judgment changes the outcome. Many people think it’s reasonable to screen out Down syndrome or cystic fibrosis. Selecting for sex, intelligence, personality or appearance feels different. The industry draws these lines too. Genomic Prediction’s co-founder, Stephen Hsu, called some traits “too controversial.” And some companies, including Orchid, only screen for disease risk and medical conditions. But Denmark and China both reshaped their populations without meaning to, whether individuals made choices that society considered “moral” or not.

How To Govern Genetic Engineering

Orchid draws one line and Nucleus another, which means the commercial limit is set by the company that’s willing to go the furthest. Today’s laws were written before screening companies advertised on subway platforms, and before startups began shopping for countries where the rules around embryo editing are ambiguous.

Preventive has explored the United Arab Emirates as a location for embryo editing, according to The Wall Street Journal . The company says its goal is preventing serious hereditary disease, not enhancement, and that it won’t pursue clinical use until safety is established.

So far, the scientific and professional response has mostly been limited to warnings. In 2025, a coalition of gene-therapy societies called for a global moratorium on heritable editing. The consortium warned that selling germline modification for enhancement or parental preference echoes “the discredited ideologies of eugenics.”

In the U.S., new reproductive tools and techniques often outpace current laws governing embryo research. Federal oversight is fragmented, and state rules vary. An annual appropriations rider prevents the FDA from accepting an application for a clinical trial involving an embryo intentionally modified to include a heritable genetic change. The bioethicist Henry Greely predicted a decade ago that people would start having their children in the lab, choosing among embryos even when they had no trouble conceiving. He told me the most obvious place to regulate is across about 500 IVF clinics where embryos are screened and implanted. He said regulating them “wouldn’t be easy,” especially since the FDA has almost no experience with them. Regulating genetics labs would likely be even harder and would raise serious questions about FDA jurisdiction. If the FDA lacks it, he said, no one else has it under current U.S. structures. In the U.K., the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority can approve or ban specific procedures. “It seems to do a pretty good job,” Greely said, though he noted it wields far more power than anything the U.S. has or is politically likely to get. Even so, a national regulator wouldn’t stop an intended parent or rogue scientist from going overseas. “I think international regulation with teeth is almost impossible,” Greely said.

“By using these technologies, we assume we can identify which traits will matter — whether the children we choose or their children’s children want that or not.”

He Jiankui went to prison under a Chinese law that didn’t directly address editing because no such law existed. He was sentenced to just three years in prison. Legal ambiguity weakens punishment after an experiment has already been conducted and doesn’t stop future attempts. The UAE’s 2023 genome law restricts the modification of human traits in embryos while allowing genetic research aimed at diseases. The law is new, and its boundaries are untested. But Preventive has been exploring the jurisdiction, where a path toward eventual clinical use may exist that the FDA rider bars in the U.S. Greely estimated it would take a couple million dollars to set up an adequate facility for a few germline edits. Cheap enough, he said, that it could happen in countries without regulation.

Greely said he sees few tools beyond “soft power condemnation and ostracism” where regulation doesn’t reach. He Jiankui became a global pariah due to a shared sense among scientists that editing a human before birth is unethical if we aren’t sure it’s safe. Much of the taboo rested on the technical dangers of CRISPR. The Columbia team’s base-editing results begin to weaken one of those safety arguments. There’s no consensus on when editing embryos for reproduction becomes safe enough to try.

What We Think We Know

When I started reporting this story, I worried that embryo screening created a simple way for culture to steer species-level evolution and tighten the feedback loop between culture and biological evolution. After talking with geneticists, anthropologists and bioethicists, I couldn’t prove it would change Homo sapiens. What I found was a tighter feedback loop than existed before, and a market sorting who can buy a potential genetic advantage.

For 300,000 years, humans adapted to situations they couldn’t predict by carrying variation no generation was aware it would need. Most cultural preferences came and went faster than they could be written into DNA. Reproductive technologies narrow that gap. “It is no longer safe to assume, as some models do, that culture is merely external to biology,” Perreault told me. “The two systems remain distinct, but they interact more directly than they once did.”

More than a decade ago, biologist Craig Venter, a key player in the effort to sequence the human genome, imagined a future in which technology could “speed up biological evolution to the pace of social evolution.” Heritable gene editing could push that acceleration further by turning a cultural preference into a genetic change in a single generation. Once a person is born from an edited embryo, that genetic change is part of their DNA and can be passed on. Reversing it in future generations would require another intervention plus the technology, money and motivation to do it. Embryo screening is more limited, but it can still influence which genetic traits a child inherits and may eventually pass down.

Today’s reproductive genetics market is global with no effective international regulator, driven by decentralized decisions as new funding, scientists and companies move toward heritable edits. If embryo screening becomes accurate and effective in another decade, it may become as routine in IVF as NIPT in pregnancy. The slow variation of biology plus the fast turnover of culture would be traded for the preferences of a single generation. There has been no collective global decision about whether this is OK. Some families will make a choice and the rest will live with whatever consequences come.

By using these technologies, we assume we can identify which traits will matter — whether the children we choose or their children’s children want that or not. A trait that looks like a benefit today could turn out to be a liability later. Today, we have an illusion of control over our genetics — we don’t know if our offspring will be improved by edits to their genes. I chose immediately and I have no idea if my choice was right. Even if the technology improves, I’m not sure the rest of us will be better off.

Tragedy on the Nepal-Tibet border. Plus: How Mark Carney stood up to Trump

Get the Guardian Weekly delivered to your home address

Over the last week, the world has watched with horror the scenes from the Tibet-Nepal border where a devastating torrent of mud, water and ice tore along the Bhotekoshi River, destroying entire communities and leaving more than 1,000 people dead and several thousand more missing.

From the Nepali town of Devighat, our south Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen describes a nightmarish scene of overflowing mortuaries and unidentifiable bodies, as shellshocked survivors of the flood slowly return to the ruins of their homes.

The disaster happened after the collapse of a glacier – and while global heating has not been definitively attributed as the cause, it is undeniable that steep mountain slopes and valleys are especially vulnerable to flooding and landslides, while extreme weather events such as monsoons and melting glaciers have become more common because of warming due to human-caused climate breakdown, as our global environment writer Jonathan Watts explains.

Then columnist Nesrine Malik paints a wider picture and argues that while for many people these floods may feel as though they have happened a world away, the climate crisis is coming for us all, one way or another.

Five essential reads in this week’s edition

Spotlight | Mark Carney shows combative nature in face-off with Trump The Canadian PM is one of the few world leaders to stand up to the US president. Former colleagues say they are not surprised. Leyland Cecco , Heather Stewart and Kalyeena Makortoff report

Science | The robots are coming! … Or are they? As entrants at the World Humanoid Games lurched from triumph to farce, Robert Booth finds that a robotics revolution may not be as close as it first appears

Interview | Gordon Brown on Burnham, billionaires – and a better Britain The former UK prime minister is still shaping politics (even if he doesn’t want to interfere). He tells Charlotte Edwardes about keeping his temper, staying fit – and why he won’t splash out for a Scotland football shirt

Opinion | The tech titans must be stripped of their power, and soon Those who said Meta harms children struck a blow, but the ability of big tech to gouge profits and cause harm is barely diminished. That’s the battle to come, argues Jonathan Freedland

Culture | Dolly Parton’s peerless career turned country music cliches inside out Beneath the wig and rhinestones, the late US country singer was the genius behind strings of classic songs that continue to inspire new artists, says Alexis Petridis

What else we’ve been reading

Stick with this fascinating and lengthy interview and you’ll want to read it again. In his interview with Mary Austen, Freddie Mercury’s former girlfriend , Simon Hattenstone meticulously documents the story his subject wants to tell but brilliantly uncovers its contradictions. One of his very best pieces. Isobel Montgomery, deputy editor

While other culinary cultures have meze or tapas or l’apéro, (some) Britons are fans of “picky bits” – a toe-curling phrase used to describe an informal meal rustled together from a fridge raid or grabbed from a supermarket chiller. I could not agree more with Laura Snapes who says the phrase should be shunned by self-respecting adults . Clare Horton, deputy editor

stories.title: Stock up on food to prepare for extreme weather, minister says
stories.summary: Dame Angela Eagle warns the weather event could lead to extreme storms this winter.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 2 hours ago

Households should stock up on food to prepare for extreme weather as the strongest El Niño event in a generation develops over the Pacific Ocean, a government minister has said.

Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle told the Guardian the powerful natural climate phenomenon will lead to "more extreme storms in this country".

Her comments came as the National Audit Office (NAO) warned Britain's food supply chain is at risk given the growing threat of cyber-attacks and the climate crisis.

The NAO said the government was too reliant on the private sector to deal with food supply disruption. The government is due to unveil a strategy about preparing for national emergencies later this year.

Dame Angela said , external : "We're about to experience probably the largest El Niño that has ever been seen, and that will lead to drier summers, wetter winters, with more extreme storms in this country.

"It will do a lot more damage in Asia with flooding, and therefore I think that we need to take it seriously.

"If you've got a store of a bit of food that can keep you going for a while before the emergency services can get to you, you're going to be a lot better off than if you haven't.

"So some of it is that kind of preparation for just being a bit more resilient."

Her comments came as an NAO report warned Britain's food supply chain is vulnerable to plant or human disease outbreaks, cyber-attacks and extreme weather.

It also cited climate change as a longer-term chronic risk which could leave Britain's food supply at risk.

The disruptions could push up prices and leave vulnerable people struggling to buy food, it said.

The NAO said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) was too reliant on private companies to handle disruptions to food supply.

It added the department had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience.

UK households are less prepared for emergencies than those in several other countries such as Finland, Sweden and European Union nations, the NAO added.

It said ministers should encourage households to prepare for supply chain disruptions and learn from the approaches taken by other countries.

Public to be told how to prepare for cyber-attack and weather emergencies Published 14 July

El Niño set to be 'strongest in living memory', says Met Office Published 21 August

Defra said the report showed food supply risks were becoming more complex and the government was working with farmers and industry to strengthen the UK's resilience.

"While our food businesses and supermarkets have continued to feed the nation through significant disruption, we will carefully consider the report's findings and recommendations as part of our ongoing work to build a more resilient, productive and sustainable food system," a spokesperson said.

In July, the government announced plans to set out the " small but important steps " households can take to prepare for food and water shortages in the event of extreme weather or cyber-attacks.

These will form a strategy to be unveiled by the end of 2026 aimed at bringing the UK closer into line with European countries in terms of emergency preparedness.

Phil Pluck, chief executive of the Cold Chain Federation, the body which represents firms transporting temperature-controlled foods, said Britain was "pretty close to crisis".

He told the BBC's Wake Up to Money programme that the country was being targeted by Russian cyber-hackers who "know that there are pinch points in the food supply system".

He added that El Niño, as well as global shipping disruption and the threat of pandemics, mean you cannot "just rely on the private sector coming through every single time".

Asked whether people should be stocking up in case of disruptions, Pluck added: "Yes, we should.

"There should be some sensible stocking in each household. And the government in the autumn will be telling all of us to do that."

stories.body:
Party podcast and social media host Ray Addison fronted films about province where China is accused of genocide

Reform UK’s top media presenter has worked for a Chinese state propaganda channel within the past year, the Guardian can reveal.

Ray Addison, who presents the political party’s in-house podcast and social media campaigns, fronted films about Xinjiang province – where the Chinese government is accused of committing genocide – for state media in September 2025.

In the videos, entitled Raymond’s Xinjiang Stories, some of which praise Chinese infrastructure, Addison described himself as a CGTN correspondent. The series was made after Addison left GB News in 2024, where he had worked as a news presenter and reporter.

Xinjiang province has attracted international attention because of alleged human rights abuses against the region’s Muslim Uyghur population by the Chinese state, including claims of forced labour, sterilisation, re-education and mass surveillance.

Addison’s work for China contrasts with the hard line Reform has taken on Chinese issues ranging from industrial relations to suspected Chinese state espionage within Westminster.

In a social media video posted by GB News in January, Nigel Farage said of the UK’s relationship with China: “I’m very, very nervous about the extent to which China has effectively spied on us, stolen many of our industrial secrets. I’m worried about the extent to which they’ve infiltrated, using money, British universities. We must be cautious about the relationship.”

The videos presented by Addison for CGTN are publicly available on YouTube and carry a warning stating that “CGTN is funded in whole or in part by the Chinese government”.

CGTN lost its licence to broadcast in the UK in 2021 after the regulator Ofcom determined it was ultimately controlled by the Chinese Communist party.

US goverments under both the previous Trump and Biden administrations have formally described China’s actions against the Uyghurs and other ethnic groups in the province as genocide . The UK government has not made a formal declaration but has noted concerns about alleged human rights abuses in the region. In 2021, British MPs voted to declare that China is committing genocide against the Uyghur people in Xinjiang.

Suella Braverman, now a Reform MP, has also made public statements to this effect. On 14 January 2025, before she defected from the Conservative party to Reform, she posted on X: “China is committing genocide in Xinjiang, funding Putin’s war of aggression in Europe and has committed acts of cyber-terrorism against the British people.”

Addison is paid by Reform to produce content about the party and creates social media videos as well as presenting its The Reform UK Podcast. In recent days he has fronted the party’s social media promotion of its conference, which is being held in Birmingham.

The party has sought to capitalise on Farage’s fanbase by advertising its podcast on the basis of exclusive interviews with the party leader and other senior party figures.

Several countries have banned or limited imports of Chinese cotton from Xinjiang because of allegations that the regime uses Uyghur slave labour to process the material.

after newsletter promotion

In one video posted on YouTube in September 2025, which appears to be filmed in Xinjiang, Addison describes the “gorgeous [cotton] fields all around me” and in solely favourable terms describes how technology is being used to boost cotton yields. He adds: “Xinjiang’s cotton story is no longer just about scale, it’s about transformation.”

Reform’s deputy leader, Richard Tice, has said the party was concerned about a range of behaviour by the Chinese Communist party, including its threat to Taiwan.

“We are very anxious about multiple areas of what China is doing, and I think we need to be much stricter on it,” he told a podcast last year. Tice went on to say that the last Conservative government had been “too permissive” of China and called for the west to make it clear to China it would “come down like a ton of bricks” both militarily and economically.

Iain Duncan Smith, one of a number of British MPs and peers targeted by Chinese sanctions, criticised Reform’s engagement of Addison. “There is a question of what due diligence will have been carried out. Everything in China is controlled by the state and if you have someone who has been employed by state media then that means they will have been employed by the state,” he said.

Reform was aware of Addison’s work for a Chinese government-controlled media outlet before he was appointed. A spokesperson did not answer specific questions about its vetting process.

A Reform spokesperson said: “Reform UK stands by its critical comments regarding China. Ray has worked for a number of British media outlets such as GB News. He has had a successful career in journalism all over the world. Ray Addison has never tried to hide where he has worked, it’s all over the internet and easily found with a Google search.”

stories.summary: About 46 people believed to be trapped in ‘room-like’ structure inside hydro plant tunnel on Nepal-Tibet border After the flood: human suffering on an unfathomable scale in Nepal’s worst-hit districts Nepal authorities have said they are “confident” that dozens of workers in Nepal’s Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant are still alive, more than a week after deadly flash floods left them trapped in an underground chamber.
